title: Chapter XXXII

teacherSummary.text: Darcy calls on Elizabeth alone and is uneasy. Charlotte suspects he is in love; Elizabeth dismisses the idea. Darcy keeps meeting her on walks.

vocabulary.etymology: “emergence”: em- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

significance: Dramatic irony: readers see what Elizabeth refuses to see.
discussionQuestions: Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXII,” how does Austen show puzzling visits? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXXII, how does Austen develop the idea of puzzling visits? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXII develops the idea of puzzling visits. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXII (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of puzzling visits. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXII suggests about puzzling visits. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's irony and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter XXXII to complicate the reader's understanding of puzzling visits. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXII within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of puzzling visits responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXII alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of puzzling visits follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXXII and its treatment of puzzling visits. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's irony and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXXII as evidence for a larger claim about puzzling visits in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXII as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of puzzling visits. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true
annotationFocus.passage: They then sat down, and when her enquiries after Rosings were made, seemed in danger of sinking into total silence. annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What clues does Elizabeth miss? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are emergence, concise, counterbalance, patronage, journeys. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “It was absolutely necessary, therefore, to think of something, and in this emergence recollecting when she had seen him last in Hertfordshire, and feeling curious to know what he would say on the subject of their hasty departure, she observed—” Webster's says: The act of rising out of a fluid, or coming forth from envelopment or concealment, or of rising into view. Now the word history: “emergence”: em- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “concise”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “counterbalance”: -ance (Latin -antia, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Unchaperoned meetings were noticeable in a small community. Why does this chapter matter? Dramatic irony: readers see what Elizabeth refuses to see. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to puzzling visits.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Foreshadowing.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
